title: Advanced Linear Algebra
subtitle: Spaces, operators, and their canonical decompositions

chapters.title: Linear systems as one matrix equation, and the operations that preserve its solutions
objectives: State the field axioms and say which one each elimination step uses
Prove that equivalent systems have the same solutions
Write each elementary row operation as multiplication by an invertible elementary matrix
Row-reduce any matrix and read the solutions of the system
chapters.prerequisites: Matrix computation and school-level elimination of linear equations.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the course promo and Lectures 1 and 2 were read in full; the running example, the proofs as written, the counterexamples and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Row-reduced echelon form: one canonical answer to every linear system
objectives: Compute the row-reduced echelon form and the matrix P with PA = R
Parametrize all solutions by the free unknowns
Decide consistency and certify inconsistency
Prove that the echelon form is unique and compare systems with it
chapters.prerequisites: Chapter 1: fields, elementary row operations, row equivalence.
chapters.source_scope: The caption of Lecture 3 was read in full; the running example, the uniqueness proof, the certificates and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Vector spaces and subspaces: the axioms that make linear combinations work
objectives: State the vector space axioms and derive their basic consequences
Verify or refute that a set with two operations is a vector space
Apply the one-step subspace test to null spaces, spans, intersections and sums
Decide when a union or a sum of subspaces is a subspace or a direct sum
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 1 and 2: fields, row reduction and solution sets.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 4 and 5 were read in full; the running matrix, the boundary examples, several proofs and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Linear independence, basis, and the invariance of dimension
objectives: Test lists of vectors for independence and spanning
Prove that all bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same size
Extend independent sets and prove the dimension formula for sums
Compute coordinates relative to an ordered basis
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 2 and 3: homogeneous systems, subspaces and spans.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 6 and 7 were read in full; the running vectors, the corrected form of the finiteness argument and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Coordinates and change of ordered basis
objectives: Compute coordinate matrices relative to an ordered basis
Build the change-of-basis matrix and apply it in the correct direction
Prove that the change-of-basis matrix is invertible and unique
Construct the ordered basis determined by an invertible matrix
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 2 and 4: invertibility by row reduction, bases and dimension.
chapters.source_scope: The caption of Lecture 8 was read in full; the polynomial running example, the second numerical example, the counting and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Row space and computations with subspaces
objectives: Prove that row operations preserve the row space
Obtain a basis, coordinates and equations of a subspace from its echelon form
Describe every invertible matrix that reduces a given matrix
Solve membership, null space, solvability and intersection problems
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 2 and 4: echelon forms, bases, dimension and coordinates.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 9 and 10 were read in full; the 5 by 5 running matrix and the small example of Section 3 are the matrices read out in those captions, and the extra theorems and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Linear transformations, null space, range, and the rank-nullity theorem
objectives: Verify linearity and compute range and null space
Define a linear map by its values on a basis and test other prescriptions
Prove the rank-nullity theorem and its consequences
Deduce that row rank equals column rank
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 2, 4 and 6: echelon forms, bases, dimension and row space.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 11 and 12 were read in full; the additional propositions, the infinite-dimensional boundary and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: The algebra of linear transformations: sums, composition, invertibility, and isomorphism
objectives: Prove that linear maps form a vector space of dimension mn
Compose linear maps and use the algebra structure of operators
Characterize invertible and nonsingular linear maps
Identify finite-dimensional spaces up to isomorphism
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 4 and 7: bases, dimension, linear maps and rank-nullity.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 13, 14 and 15 were read in full; the running matrices, the one-sided inverse examples and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Matrix representation of linear transformations and similarity
objectives: Compute the matrix of a linear map relative to ordered bases
Prove that representation is a linear isomorphism that turns composition into product
Derive the change-of-basis and similarity formulas
Use invariants to separate non-similar matrices
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 5, 7 and 8: coordinates, linear maps and their algebra, and determinants.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 16 and 17 were read in full; the second numerical computation completes an example left open there, and the running matrix and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Linear functionals, dual spaces, and dual bases
objectives: Recognize and compute linear functionals
Construct the dual basis and use it to read coordinates
Prove the dimension formula for annihilators
Describe subspaces as intersections of hyperspaces
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 4, 6, 7 and 8: bases, row reduction, linear maps and L(V,W).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 18, 19 and 20 were read in full; the numerical examples, the lower bound on hyperspaces and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Annihilators, the double dual, and the transpose of a linear map
objectives: Prove that a finite-dimensional space is canonically isomorphic to its double dual
Show that every basis of the dual space is a dual basis
Relate kernel and range of the transpose to annihilators
Prove that the matrix of the transpose is the transposed matrix
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 7, 9 and 10: rank-nullity, matrices of linear maps and dual bases.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 21 and 22 were read in full; the running matrix, the solvability criterion, the infinite-dimensional examples and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and the characteristic polynomial
objectives: Define eigenvalues and eigenspaces and compute them
Prove the properties of the characteristic polynomial
Prove independence of eigenvectors and the multiplicity bound
Decide diagonalizability from eigenspace dimensions
chapters.prerequisites: Determinants, and Chapters 2, 7 and 9: row reduction, kernels and similarity.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 23 and 24 were read in full; the two matrices are read out in them, and the growth comparison, the added theorems and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Diagonalizable operators and annihilating polynomials
objectives: Prove that eigenspaces of distinct eigenvalues are independent
Characterize diagonalizability by eigenspace dimensions
Construct the minimal polynomial and prove its properties
Prove the distinct-linear-factor criterion in both directions
chapters.prerequisites: Chapters 8, 9 and 12: operator spaces, similarity and eigenvalues.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 25 and 26 were read in full; the second matrix, the converse proof by Lagrange polynomials and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem and the minimal polynomial in computation
objectives: Prove the Cayley-Hamilton theorem through the adjugate
Compute powers and inverses from annihilating polynomials
Compare the spectra and minimal polynomials of AB and BA
Decide diagonalizability over different fields
chapters.prerequisites: Determinants and adjugates, and Chapters 12 and 13: characteristic and minimal polynomials.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of Lectures 27 and 28 were read in full; the matrices of the main examples are read out in them, and the divisibility theorem for AB and BA, the field extensions and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Invariant subspaces, conductors, and triangulability
objectives: Test invariance of a subspace and read the resulting block form
Relate the polynomials of a restriction to those of the operator
Compute conductors into invariant subspaces and prove their properties
Use the linear-conductor lemma and the flag form of triangularity
chapters.prerequisites: Bases, matrices of operators, eigenvalues, determinants, the minimal polynomial and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem (Chapters 4 to 14).
chapters.source_scope: Read: the stored caption texts at positions 30 and 31. The stored text at position 30 duplicates the transpose lecture at position 23, so the invariant-subspace topics of that recording were taken from YouTube's automatic English captions for the same video. The running example, extended proofs, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Applications of invariant subspaces: diagonalizability criteria and simultaneous triangulation
objectives: Prove that an operator is triangulable exactly when its minimal polynomial splits
Prove the distinct-linear-factor criterion for diagonalizability
Construct triangularizing bases and test the criteria on examples
Triangularize a commuting family with one basis
chapters.prerequisites: Invariant subspaces and conductors (Chapter 15), the minimal polynomial and eigenvalues (Chapters 12 to 14).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 32 and 33) were read in full. The running matrix and the integral-operator example come from them; the commuting-family section, the extended proofs, the laboratory and the exercises are additions.

chapters.title: Direct-sum decompositions and projections
objectives: Prove the equivalent criteria for independent subspaces
Construct the projection on one summand along another
Characterize direct-sum decompositions by families of projections
Read the block-diagonal form from invariant summands
chapters.prerequisites: Bases, dimension, linear operators and invariant subspaces (Chapters 3, 4, 7 and 15).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 34 and 35) were read in full. The plane projection example and the symmetric-matrix and eigenspace examples come from them; the running 3 by 3 operator, extra proofs, counterexamples, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Invariant direct sums and block-diagonal operators
objectives: Prove that invariant summands are detected by commuting projections
Write a diagonalizable operator in spectral form and compute polynomials of it
Express the spectral projections as Lagrange polynomials in the operator
Prove that a spectral form implies diagonalizability
chapters.prerequisites: Direct sums and projections (Chapter 17), eigenvalues and diagonalizability (Chapters 12, 13 and 16).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 36 and 37) were read in full. The running operator, the uniqueness and minimal-polynomial corollaries, boundary cases, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: The primary decomposition theorem
objectives: State the primary decomposition theorem over an arbitrary field
Build the component projections from a Bezout identity
Prove that each restriction has a prime-power minimal polynomial
Apply the decomposition to invariant subspaces and generalized eigenspaces
chapters.prerequisites: Minimal polynomial, polynomial ideals, direct sums and projections (Chapters 13 and 15 to 18).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 38 and 39) were read in full. The 3 by 3 block of the running example is the matrix discussed in the first recording; the quarter-turn block, the corollaries, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Applications of primary decomposition: diagonalizable plus nilpotent parts
objectives: Solve linear initial value problems with generalized eigenvector chains
Prove existence and uniqueness of the diagonalizable-plus-nilpotent splitting
Prove the cyclic decomposition for a prime-power minimal polynomial
Compute Jordan and rational canonical forms
chapters.prerequisites: The primary decomposition theorem (Chapter 19), diagonalizability and direct sums (Chapters 16 to 18).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the three recordings (positions 40 to 42) were read in full. The 2 by 2 system and the six- and eight-dimensional examples follow them; the running matrix is from Chapter 12; the proofs of the canonical-form theorems, the laboratory and the exercises are original.

chapters.title: Inner products, norms, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
objectives: Verify the inner product axioms and use the conjugation convention
Represent an inner product by a positive definite Gram matrix
Prove the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities
Orthogonalize an independent list by Gram-Schmidt
chapters.prerequisites: Vector spaces, bases, coordinates and matrices over the real or complex numbers.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the four recordings (positions 43, 44, 61 and 45) were read in full. The standard examples, the Hilbert matrix, the twisted inner product, the trigonometric system and the three-dimensional Gram-Schmidt data come from them; the polynomial running example, extra proofs, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Orthogonal projection, Gram-Schmidt, and best approximation
objectives: Characterize best approximations by orthogonality
Compute projections by orthogonal bases and by normal equations
Prove the direct sum of a finite-dimensional subspace and its orthogonal complement
Prove Bessel's inequality and see where existence fails
chapters.prerequisites: Inner products, orthogonal sets and Gram-Schmidt (Chapter 21); projections (Chapter 17).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 47 and 46) were read in full. The line example comes from the first; the running plane, normal equations, the infinite-dimensional counterexample, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Linear functionals and adjoint operators on inner product spaces
objectives: Represent linear functionals by vectors and find the vector
Construct the adjoint and compute its matrix in any basis
Prove the algebraic rules of adjoints and decompose operators
Recognize the failure of both existence theorems in infinite dimension
chapters.prerequisites: Inner products and orthonormal bases (Chapters 21 and 22); dual spaces and transposes (Chapter 11).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the four recordings (positions 48 to 51) were read in full. The evaluation example, the projection onto a line, the matrix, trace, multiplication and differentiation examples come from them; the derivative adjoint on quadratics, the general-basis formula, the transpose relation, the range-kernel facts, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Inner-product-space isomorphisms and unitary operators
objectives: Characterize isomorphisms of inner product spaces
Relate unitary operators to adjoints and unitary matrices
Factor an invertible matrix into triangular and unitary factors
Derive the necessary conditions for an orthonormal eigenbasis
chapters.prerequisites: Gram-Schmidt (Chapter 21) and adjoint operators (Chapter 23).
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the four recordings (positions 52, 53, 55 and 54) were read in full. The weighted function-space example, matrix cases and the three-dimensional factorization family come from them; the running matrix, shift example, Schur consequence, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Normal operators and spectral resolution
objectives: Prove that self-adjoint operators have orthonormal eigenbases
Relate eigenvectors of a normal operator and its adjoint
Prove Schur's theorem and the spectral theorem
Compute spectral resolutions and polynomials of operators
chapters.prerequisites: Adjoints (Chapter 23), unitary and self-adjoint operators (Chapter 24), eigenvalues and projections.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the three recordings (positions 56 to 58) were read in full. The multiplication-operator example comes from the first; the running symmetric matrix, the rotation-dilation matrix, laboratory and exercises are original.

chapters.title: Singular value decomposition and forms on inner product spaces
objectives: Prove and compute the singular value decomposition
Correspond sesquilinear forms with operators
Distinguish the matrix of a form from the matrix of an operator
Diagonalize Hermitian forms by principal axes
chapters.prerequisites: The spectral theorem (Chapter 25), the representation theorem (Chapter 23) and Gram-Schmidt.
chapters.source_scope: The captions of the two recordings (positions 59 and 60) were read in full. The three by two example comes from the first; the running matrix, positivity criterion, change-of-basis rules, laboratory and exercises are original.
